title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Pierre, having decided that until he carried out his plan he would reveal neither his identity nor his knowledge of French, stood at the half-open corridor door, intending to hide as soon as the French entered. But the French came in, and still Pierre did not retreat—an irresistible curiosity kept him there.

There were two of them. One was an officer—a tall, soldierly, handsome man—the other evidently a private or an orderly, sunburned, short, and thin, with sunken cheeks and a dull expression. The officer walked in front, leaning on a stick and limping slightly. When he had advanced a few steps, he stopped, apparently having decided these were good quarters, turned to the soldiers standing at the entrance, and in a loud voice ordered them to stable the horses. Having done that, the officer, lifting his elbow with a smart gesture, stroked his mustache and lightly touched his hat.
"Good day, everybody!" he said gaily, smiling and looking about him.
* "Good day, everybody!"
No one answered.
"Are you the master here?" the officer asked Gerasim.
* "Are you the master here?"
Gerasim gazed at the officer with an alarmed and questioning look.

"Quarters, quarters, lodgings!" said the officer, looking down at the little man with a condescending, good-natured smile. "The French are good fellows. Come now! Don't let's be cross, old fellow!" he added, clapping the scared and silent Gerasim on the shoulder. "Well, does no one speak French in this establishment?" he asked again in French, looking around and meeting Pierre's eyes. Pierre moved away from the door.
* "Quarters, quarters, lodgings! The French are good fellows. What the devil! There, don't let us be cross, old fellow!"
Again the officer turned to Gerasim and asked him to show him the rooms in the house.
"Master, not here—don't understand... me, you..." said Gerasim, trying to make his words more comprehensible by distorting them.

Still smiling, the French officer spread out his hands before Gerasim's nose, indicating that he didn't understand him either, and moved, limping, to the door where Pierre was standing. Pierre wanted to go away and hide, but at that moment he saw Makar Alexeevich appearing at the open kitchen door with the pistol in his hand. With a madman's cunning, Makar Alexeevich eyed the Frenchman, raised his pistol, and took aim.

"Board them!" yelled the tipsy man, trying to pull the trigger. Hearing the yell, the officer turned around, and at the same moment Pierre threw himself at the drunkard. Just as Pierre grabbed and knocked up the pistol, Makar Alexeevich finally got his fingers on the trigger—there was a deafening report, and everything was enveloped in a cloud of smoke. The Frenchman turned pale and rushed to the door.
Forgetting his intention of concealing his knowledge of French, Pierre snatched away the pistol, threw it down, ran up to the officer, and addressed him in French.
"You are not wounded?" he asked.

"I think not," answered the Frenchman, feeling himself over. "But I've had a lucky escape this time," he added, pointing to the damaged plaster on the wall. "Who is that man?" he asked, looking sternly at Pierre.
"Oh, I am truly sorry about what has happened," said Pierre quickly, completely forgetting the role he had meant to play. "He is an unfortunate madman who did not know what he was doing."
The officer went up to Makar Alexeevich and took him by the collar.
Makar Alexeevich was standing with parted lips, swaying as if about to fall asleep, leaning against the wall.

"Scoundrel! You shall pay for this," said the Frenchman, letting go of him. "We French are merciful after victory, but we do not pardon traitors," he added, with a look of gloomy dignity and a fine, dramatic gesture.

Pierre continued, in French, to persuade the officer not to hold the drunken imbecile accountable. The Frenchman listened in silence with the same gloomy expression, but suddenly turned to Pierre with a smile. For a few seconds he looked at him in silence. His handsome face assumed a melodramatically gentle expression and he held out his hand.
"You have saved my life. You are French," said he.

For a Frenchman, that conclusion was indisputable. Only a Frenchman could perform a great deed, and to save his life—the life of Monsieur Ramballe, captain of the 13th Light Regiment—was undoubtedly a very great deed.
But however certain that conclusion and the officer's conviction based upon it, Pierre felt it necessary to correct him.
"I am Russian," he said quickly.

"Oh, come now! Tell that to others," said the officer, waving his finger before his nose and smiling. "You shall tell me all about that later. I am delighted to meet a compatriot. Well, and what are we to do with this man?" he added, addressing Pierre as a brother.

Even if Pierre were not a Frenchman, having once received that loftiest of human titles, he could not renounce it—the officer's look and tone said as much. In reply to his last question, Pierre again explained who Makar Alexeevich was and how just before their arrival the drunken imbecile had seized the loaded pistol which they had not had time to take from him, and he begged the officer to let the deed go unpunished.
The Frenchman puffed out his chest and made a grand gesture with his arm.

"You have saved my life! You are French. You ask his pardon? I grant it. Lead that man away!" he said quickly and energetically, and taking the arm of Pierre—whom he had promoted to the status of Frenchman for saving his life—he went with him into the room.
The soldiers in the yard, hearing the shot, came into the corridor asking what had happened, and expressed their readiness to punish the culprit, but the officer sternly stopped them.
"You will be called when you are wanted," he said.
The soldiers went out again, and the orderly, who had meanwhile had time to visit the kitchen, came up to his officer.
"Captain, there is soup and a leg of mutton in the kitchen," said he. "Shall I serve them up?"
"Yes, and some wine," answered the captain.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 32
paragraphs: Seven days had passed since Prince Andrew found himself at the field hospital on the battlefield of Borodino. His feverish state and the inflammation of his injured bowels, the doctor believed, would certainly kill him. But on the seventh day he ate a piece of bread with some tea with pleasure, and the doctor noticed that his temperature was lower. He had regained consciousness that morning. The first night after they left Moscow had been fairly warm and he had remained in the carriage, but at Mytishchi the wounded man himself asked to be taken out and given some tea. The pain caused by being moved into the hut made him groan aloud and lose consciousness again. When he had been placed on his camp bed, he lay for a long time motionless with closed eyes. Then he opened them and whispered softly: "And the tea?" Remembering such a small, everyday detail astonished the doctor. He felt Prince Andrew's pulse and, to his surprise and dissatisfaction, found it had improved. He was dissatisfied because he knew from experience that if his patient did not die now, he would die a little later with greater suffering. Timokhin, the red-nosed major from Prince Andrew's regiment, had joined him in Moscow and was being taken along, having been wounded in the leg at Borodino. They were accompanied by a doctor, Prince Andrew's valet, his coachman, and two orderlies.
They gave Prince Andrew some tea. He drank it eagerly, looking with feverish eyes at the door before him as if trying to understand and remember something.
"I don't want any more. Is Timokhin here?" he asked.
Timokhin crept along the bench toward him.
"I am here, your excellency."
"How's your wound?"
"Mine, sir? All right. But how about you?"
Prince Andrew pondered again as if trying to remember something.
"Couldn't someone get me a book?" he asked.
"What book?"
"The Gospels. I don't have one."

The doctor promised to get it for him and began asking how he was feeling. Prince Andrew answered all his questions reluctantly but reasonably, then said he wanted a bolster placed under him because he was uncomfortable and in great pain. The doctor and valet lifted the cloak covering him and, making wry faces at the terrible smell of mortifying flesh that came from the wound, began examining that dreadful place. The doctor was very much displeased about something and made a change in the dressings, turning the wounded man over so that he groaned again and grew unconscious and delirious from the agony. He kept asking them to get him the book and put it under him.
"What trouble would it be to you?" he said. "I don't have one. Please get it for me and put it underneath for a moment," he pleaded in a piteous voice.
The doctor went into the passage to wash his hands.
"You people have no conscience," said he to the valet who was pouring water over his hands. "I turn my back for one moment... It's such pain, you know, I'm amazed he can bear it."
"By the Lord Jesus Christ, I thought we had put something under him!" said the valet.

The first time Prince Andrew understood where he was and what had happened, and remembered being wounded, was when he asked to be carried into the hut after his carriage had stopped at Mytishchi. After growing confused from pain while being carried in, he again regained consciousness, and while drinking tea once more recalled everything that had happened to him, and above all vividly remembered the moment at the field hospital when, at the sight of the suffering of a man he disliked, those new thoughts had come to him—thoughts that promised happiness. And those thoughts, though now vague and indefinite, again filled his soul. He remembered that he had a new source of happiness, and that this happiness had something to do with the Gospels. That was why he asked for a copy. The uncomfortable position they had put him in and turned him over again confused his thoughts, and when he came to himself a third time, it was in the complete stillness of the night. Everyone near him was sleeping. A cricket chirped from across the passage; someone was shouting and singing in the street; cockroaches rustled on the table, on the icons, and on the walls, and a big fly buzzed at the head of the bed and around the candle beside him, its wick charred and shaped like a mushroom.

His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy person usually thinks of, feels, and remembers countless things simultaneously, but has the power and will to select one sequence of thoughts or events on which to focus all his attention. A healthy person can tear himself away from the deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who enters, and then return to his own thoughts. But Prince Andrew's mind was not in a normal state in that respect. All the powers of his mind were more active and clearer than ever, but they operated apart from his will. The most diverse thoughts and images occupied him simultaneously. At times his brain suddenly began to work with a vigor, clarity, and depth it had never reached when he was healthy, but suddenly in the midst of its work it would turn to some unexpected idea and he lacked the strength to return to the first.

"Yes, a new happiness was revealed to me—one that cannot be taken from a person," he thought as he lay in the semi-darkness of the quiet hut, gazing fixedly before him with feverish, wide-open eyes. "A happiness lying beyond material forces, beyond the material influences that act on a person—a happiness of the soul alone, the happiness of loving. Every person can understand it, but only God could conceive and command it. But how did God command that law? And why was the Son...?"

And suddenly the sequence of these thoughts broke off, and Prince Andrew heard (without knowing whether it was a delusion or reality) a soft whispering voice incessantly and rhythmically repeating "piti-piti-piti," and then "titi," and then again "piti-piti-piti," and "ti-ti" once more. At the same time he felt that above his face, above the very middle of it, some strange airy structure was being built out of slender needles or splinters, to the sound of this whispered music. He felt that he had to balance carefully (though it was difficult) so that this airy structure would not collapse; but nevertheless it kept collapsing and again slowly rising to the sound of the whispered rhythmic music—"it stretches, stretches, spreading out and stretching," said Prince Andrew to himself. While listening to this whispering and feeling the sensation of drawing out and the construction of this needle-like edifice, he also saw by glimpses a red halo around the candle, and heard the rustle of the cockroaches and the buzzing of the fly that bumped against his pillow and face. Each time the fly touched his face it gave him a burning sensation, and yet to his surprise it did not destroy the structure, though it hit the very spot where it was rising. But besides all this there was something else of importance. It was something white by the door—the statue of a sphinx, which also oppressed him.

"But perhaps that's my shirt on the table," he thought, "and those are my legs, and that is the door, but why is it always stretching and drawing itself out, and 'piti-piti-piti' and 'ti-ti' and 'piti-piti-piti'...? That's enough, please stop!" Prince Andrew painfully entreated someone. And suddenly thoughts and feelings again surfaced in his mind with peculiar clarity and force.

"Yes—love," he thought again quite clearly. "But not love that loves for something, for some quality, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love which I—while dying—first experienced when I saw my enemy and yet loved him. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and does not require an object. Now again I feel that bliss. To love one's neighbors, to love one's enemies, to love everything—to love God in all His forms. It is possible to love someone dear to you with human love, but an enemy can only be loved by divine love. That is why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?...

"When loving with human love one may pass from love to hatred, but divine love cannot change. No, neither death nor anything else can destroy it. It is the very essence of the soul. Yet how many people have I hated in my life? And of them all, I loved and hated none as I did her." And he vividly pictured Natasha to himself, not as he had done in the past with nothing but her charms which gave him pleasure, but for the first time picturing her soul. And he understood her feelings, her suffering, her shame, and her remorse. He now understood for the first time all the cruelty of his rejection of her, the cruelty of his break with her. "If only it were possible to see her once more! Just once, looking into those eyes to say..."

"Piti-piti-piti and ti-ti and piti-piti-piti boom!" buzzed the fly... And his attention was suddenly carried into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something was happening. In that world some structure was still being built and did not fall, something was still stretching out, and the candle with its red halo was still burning, and the same shirt-like sphinx lay near the door; but besides all this something creaked, there was a breath of fresh air, and a new white sphinx appeared, standing at the door. And that sphinx had the pale face and shining eyes of the very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

"Oh, how oppressive this constant delirium is," thought Prince Andrew, trying to drive that face from his imagination. But the face remained before him with the force of reality and drew nearer. Prince Andrew wished to return to that former world of pure thought, but he could not, and delirium drew him back. The soft whispering voice continued its rhythmic murmur, something pressed on him and stretched out, and the strange face was before him. Prince Andrew gathered all his strength in an effort to recover his senses; he moved a little, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, a dimness in his eyes, and like a man plunged into water he lost consciousness. When he came to himself, Natasha—that same living Natasha whom of all people he most longed to love with this new, pure, divine love that had been revealed to him—was kneeling before him. He realized it was the real, living Natasha, and he was not surprised but quietly happy. Natasha, motionless on her knees (she could not move), with frightened eyes fixed on him, was holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and rigid. Only in the lower part of it something quivered.
Prince Andrew sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.
"You?" he said. "How fortunate!"
With a quick but careful movement, Natasha drew closer to him on her knees and, taking his hand gently, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.
"Forgive me!" she whispered, raising her head and glancing at him. "Forgive me!"
"I love you," said Prince Andrew.
"Forgive...!"
"Forgive what?" he asked.
"Forgive me for what I ha-ve do-ne!" Natasha faltered in a scarcely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more quickly, just touching it with her lips.
"I love you more, better than before," said Prince Andrew, lifting her face with his hand so he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, filled with happy tears, gazed at him shyly, compassionately, and with joyous love. Natasha's thin pale face, with its swollen lips, was more than plain—it was awful. But Prince Andrew did not see that; he saw her shining eyes, which were beautiful. They heard the sound of voices behind them.

Peter the valet, now wide awake, had roused the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything, carefully covering his bare body with the sheet as he huddled on his bench.
"What's this?" said the doctor, rising from his bed. "Please go away, madam!"
At that moment a maid sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter's absence, knocked at the door.
Like a sleepwalker awakened from her sleep, Natasha went out of the room and, returning to her hut, fell sobbing on her bed.

From that time on, during all the rest of the Rostovs' journey, at every stop and wherever they spent a night, Natasha never left the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected such firmness or such skill in nursing from a young girl.

Dreadful as the countess imagined it would be should Prince Andrew die in her daughter's arms during the journey—as, judging by what the doctor said, seemed possible—she could not oppose Natasha. Though with the intimacy now established between the wounded man and Natasha the thought occurred that should he recover their former engagement would be renewed, no one—least of all Natasha and Prince Andrew—spoke of this. The unsettled question of life and death, which hung not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, shut out every other consideration.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: The famous flank movement was really quite simple: after the French advance had stopped, the Russian army—which had been retreating straight back from the invaders—veered away from that direct line and, finding it wasn't being pursued, naturally drifted toward the region where supplies were most plentiful.

If instead of imagining genius commanders leading the Russian army, we picture that army without any leaders at all, it couldn't have done anything but swing back toward Moscow in an arc toward the areas where food was most abundant and the land was richest.

This shift from the Nizhni toward the Ryazan, Tula, and Kaluga roads was so natural that even Russian stragglers moved in that direction, and orders were sent from Petersburg for Kutuzov to take this very route. At Tarutino, Kutuzov received what amounted to a reprimand from the Emperor for moving along the Ryazan road, with the Emperor's letter pointing him toward the very position near Kaluga that he had already occupied.

Having rolled like a ball in the direction given by the momentum of the whole campaign and the Battle of Borodino, the Russian army—when that momentum was spent and no fresh push came—settled into its natural position.

Kutuzov's merit lay not in any so-called strategic masterstroke but in the fact that he alone understood the significance of what had happened. He alone grasped the meaning of the French army's inactivity. He alone continued to insist that the Battle of Borodino had been a victory. He alone—though as commander in chief he might have been expected to be eager to attack—used all his strength to hold the Russian army back from pointless engagements.

The beast wounded at Borodino was lying where the fleeing hunter had left it. Whether it was still alive, whether it was strong and merely lying low—the hunter didn't know. Suddenly the beast was heard to moan.
The moan of that wounded beast—the French army—which revealed its desperate condition, was the sending of Lauriston to Kutuzov's camp with peace proposals.
Napoleon, with his usual certainty that whatever entered his head was right, wrote to Kutuzov the first words that came to mind, though they meant nothing.

'My Prince Kutuzov: I am sending one of my adjutants-general to discuss several interesting questions with you. I beg Your Highness to believe what he says, especially when he expresses the sentiments of esteem and special regard I have long held for your person. This letter having no other purpose, I pray God to keep you in His holy and gracious protection!'
NAPOLEON
Moscow, October 30, 1812

Kutuzov replied: 'I would be cursed by future generations if I were seen as the one who initiated any kind of settlement. Such is the spirit of my nation.' But he continued to use all his powers to keep his troops from attacking.

During the month the French troops spent looting Moscow while the Russian troops rested quietly at Tarutino, a shift had taken place in the relative strength of the two armies—both in spirit and in numbers—so that the advantage had passed to the Russian side. Although the Russians didn't know the exact condition and numbers of the French army, as soon as this shift occurred, the need to attack became obvious through countless signs: Lauriston's mission, the abundance of supplies at Tarutino, the reports pouring in from all sides about French disorder and inactivity, the flow of recruits into Russian regiments, the fine weather, the long rest the Russian soldiers had enjoyed, the natural impatience to do what they'd been assembled for, curiosity about what the French army was doing, the boldness of Russian outposts scouting close to the French positions at Tarutino, news of easy victories by peasants and guerrillas, the envy this aroused, the desire for revenge that burned in every Russian heart while the French remained in Moscow, and above all a dim awareness in every soldier's mind that the balance of power had shifted and the advantage was now theirs. A real change had occurred, and an advance had become inevitable. And at once—just as a clock begins to strike and chime when the minute hand completes its circle—this change showed itself through increased activity, buzzing, and ringing in the higher command.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Early in the morning of October sixth, Pierre went out of the shed and, on his way back, stopped by the door to play with a little blue-gray dog with a long body and short, bowed legs that was jumping around him. This little dog lived in their shed, sleeping beside Karataev at night. It sometimes wandered into town but always came back. It had probably never had an owner—it belonged to nobody and had no name. The French called it Azor; the soldier who told stories called it Femgalka; Karataev and the others called it Gray, or sometimes Flabby. Having no master, no name, and not even a definite breed or color didn't seem to bother the blue-gray dog in the least. Its furry tail stood up firm and round like a plume, its crooked little legs served it so well that it would often gracefully lift a hind leg and trot along quickly on three legs, as if disdaining to use all four. Everything pleased it. One moment it would roll on its back yelping with delight, the next it would bask in the sun with an air of self-important thoughtfulness, then frolic around playing with a stick or a piece of straw.

Pierre's outfit now consisted of a dirty, torn shirt (the only remnant of his former clothing), a pair of soldier's trousers that he tied at the ankles with string on Karataev's advice for warmth, and a peasant coat and cap. He had changed a great deal physically. He no longer looked stout, though he still had the solid, strong build that ran in his family. A beard and mustache covered the lower part of his face, and a tangle of hair, infested with lice, curled around his head like a cap. The look in his eyes was resolute, calm, and alertly alive—unlike anything before. The old slackness that had shown even in his eyes was now replaced by an energetic readiness for action and resistance. His feet were bare.

Pierre first looked across the field where vehicles and riders were passing that morning, then into the distance across the river, then at the dog pretending to seriously bite him, and then down at his own bare feet, which he placed in various positions with obvious pleasure, wiggling his dirty, thick big toes. Every time he looked at his bare feet, a smile of amused self-satisfaction crossed his face. The sight of them reminded him of everything he had experienced and learned during these weeks, and the memory was pleasant.
For several days the weather had been calm and clear, with slight frosts in the morning—what people call an 'old wives' summer.'
In the sunshine the air was warm, and that warmth was especially pleasant alongside the invigorating freshness of the morning frost still lingering in the air.

On everything near and far lay that magical crystal shimmer you see only in autumn. The Sparrow Hills were visible in the distance—the village, the church, the large white house. The bare trees, the sand, the bricks and rooftops, the green church spire, and the corners of the white house all stood out in the transparent air with an unnaturally delicate clarity. Nearby were the familiar ruins of a half-burned mansion occupied by the French, with lilac bushes still showing dark green beside the fence. Even that ruined, defiled house—repulsively ugly in dull weather—looked quietly beautiful now in the clear, motionless light.
A French corporal, his coat unbuttoned in a homey way, a skullcap on his head and a short pipe in his mouth, came around the corner of the shed and approached Pierre with a friendly wink.
'What sunshine, Monsieur Kiril!' (That was their name for Pierre.) 'Just like spring!'
And the corporal leaned against the door and offered Pierre his pipe, though Pierre always declined it.
'To be on the march in such weather...' he began.

Pierre asked what was being said about leaving, and the corporal told him that nearly all the troops were departing and there should be orders about the prisoners that day. Sokolov, one of the soldiers sharing Pierre's shed, was dying, and Pierre told the corporal that something should be done about him. The corporal replied that Pierre needn't worry—they had an ambulance and a hospital, and arrangements would be made for the sick. In general, everything that could happen had been anticipated by the authorities.

'Besides, Monsieur Kiril, you only have to say a word to the captain, you know. He's a man who never forgets anything. Have a word with the captain when he makes his rounds—he'll do anything for you.'
(The captain the corporal mentioned often had long conversations with Pierre and showed him all kinds of favors.)

'"You see, St. Thomas," he said to me the other day, "Monsieur Kiril is an educated man who speaks French. He's a Russian gentleman who's had bad luck, but he's a real man. He knows what's what. If he needs anything and asks me, he won't be refused. When a man has had an education, you see, he appreciates learning and well-bred people." I mention this for your sake, Monsieur Kiril. The other day, if it hadn't been for you, that business would have ended badly.'

After chatting a while longer, the corporal went away. (The incident he'd mentioned had happened a few days earlier—a fight between the prisoners and the French soldiers, in which Pierre had managed to calm his comrades down.) Some prisoners who had overheard Pierre talking to the corporal immediately asked what the Frenchman had said. While Pierre was relaying the news about the army leaving Moscow, a thin, sallow, ragged French soldier came to the shed door. Quickly and timidly raising his fingers to his forehead in greeting, he asked Pierre whether the soldier Platoche—to whom he had given a shirt to sew—was in this shed.
A week earlier, the French had been issued boot leather and linen, which they'd given to the prisoners to make into boots and shirts.
'Ready, ready, my friend!' said Karataev, coming out with a neatly folded shirt.

Karataev, because of the warm weather and for ease of work, was wearing only trousers and a tattered shirt as black as soot. His hair was tied up workman-style with a strip of lime bark, and his round face looked rounder and more pleasant than ever.
'A promise is a sacred thing! I said Friday, and here it is—ready,' said Platon, smiling as he unfolded the shirt he had sewn.

The Frenchman glanced around nervously, then, as if overcoming his hesitation, quickly pulled off his uniform and put on the shirt. Under the uniform, next to his sallow, thin bare body, he wore a long, greasy, flowered silk waistcoat—but no shirt. He was clearly afraid the watching prisoners would laugh at him, and thrust his head into the shirt quickly. None of the prisoners said a word.
'See, it fits nicely!' Platon kept saying, smoothing the shirt straight.
The Frenchman pushed his head and hands through without looking up, examining the shirt and checking the seams.

'You know, my friend, this isn't a tailor's shop, and I didn't have the right tools. As they say, you need the proper tool even to crack a louse,' said Platon with one of his warm, round smiles, clearly pleased with his work.
'It's good, quite good, thank you,' said the Frenchman in French, 'but there must be some fabric left over.'
'It'll fit even better once it settles to your body,' said Karataev, still admiring his handiwork. 'You'll be nice and comfortable...'
'Thanks, thanks, old fellow... But the leftover pieces?' the Frenchman said again, smiling. He took out a ruble note and gave it to Karataev. 'But give me the scraps that are left.'

Pierre saw that Platon didn't want to understand what the Frenchman was saying, and he watched without interfering. Karataev thanked the Frenchman for the money and went on admiring his own work. The Frenchman insisted on getting back the leftover material and asked Pierre to translate.
'What does he want the scraps for?' said Karataev. 'They'd make fine leg wrappings for us. Well, never mind.'

And Karataev, his face suddenly changed and saddened, took a small bundle of scraps from inside his shirt and handed it to the Frenchman without looking at him. 'Oh well!' he muttered, and walked away. The Frenchman looked at the cloth, thought for a moment, then glanced inquiringly at Pierre and—as if Pierre's expression told him something—suddenly blushed and shouted in a squeaky voice:
'Platoche! Hey, Platoche! Keep them yourself!' And handing back the scraps, he turned and walked out.

'There, look at that,' said Karataev, shaking his head. 'People said they weren't Christians, but they have souls too. It's what the old folks used to say: "A sweating hand is an open hand, a dry hand is a tight one." He's got nothing himself, but he gave them back.'
Karataev smiled thoughtfully and sat quietly for a while, looking at the pieces of cloth.
'But they'll make wonderful leg wrappings, my friend,' he said, and went back into the shed.

title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Throughout the entire march from Moscow, no new orders had been given by the French authorities regarding the group of prisoners that included Pierre. By October twenty-second, their party was no longer traveling with the same troops and supply wagons they had left Moscow with. Half the hardtack wagons that had accompanied them on the first legs of the journey had been captured by Cossacks; the other half had gone on ahead. Not one of the dismounted cavalrymen who had marched at the front of the prisoner column remained—they had all disappeared. The artillery the prisoners had seen ahead of them during the early days had been replaced by Marshal Junot's enormous baggage train, escorted by Westphalians. Behind the prisoners came a cavalry baggage train.

From Vyazma onward, the French army, which had until then been moving in three columns, continued as a single mass. The symptoms of disorder that Pierre had first noticed at their initial stopping place after leaving Moscow had now reached their ultimate extreme.

The road they traveled was bordered on both sides by dead horses. Ragged men who had fallen behind from various regiments constantly drifted in and out, sometimes joining the moving column, sometimes dropping behind again.

Several times during the march, false alarms had been raised. The escort soldiers would grab their muskets, fire, and run in a panic, trampling one another, only to reassemble afterward and curse each other for the needless fright.
These three groups traveling together—the cavalry stores, the convoy of prisoners, and Junot's baggage train—still formed a separate and unified whole, though each group was rapidly shrinking.

Of the artillery baggage train, which had originally consisted of a hundred and twenty wagons, no more than sixty remained; the rest had been captured or abandoned. Several of Junot's wagons had also been seized or left behind. Three wagons had been raided and looted by stragglers from Davout's corps. From the talk of the Germans, Pierre learned that a larger guard had been assigned to that baggage train than to the prisoners, and that one of their comrades, a German soldier, had been shot on the marshal's direct order because a silver spoon belonging to the marshal had been found in his possession.

The group of prisoners had shrunk the most. Of the three hundred and thirty men who had set out from Moscow, fewer than a hundred now remained. The prisoners were more burdensome to their escort than even the cavalry saddles or Junot's baggage. They all understood that the saddles and Junot's spoon might have some use, but that cold and hungry soldiers should have to stand guard over equally cold and hungry Russians who kept freezing and collapsing on the road—at which point the order was to shoot them—was not merely incomprehensible but revolting. And the escort, as if afraid that giving in to the pity they felt for the prisoners would only make their own situation worse, treated them with particular harshness and cruelty.

At Dorogobuzhsk, while the convoy soldiers had locked the prisoners in a stable and gone off to loot their own supply stores, several prisoner soldiers tunneled under the wall and escaped, but they were recaptured by the French and shot.

The earlier arrangement of keeping officer prisoners separate from the rest had long since been abandoned. All who could walk went together, and after the third stage Pierre had rejoined Karataev and the gray-blue, bandy-legged dog that had adopted Karataev as its master.

On the third day after leaving Moscow, Karataev fell ill again with the fever he had suffered from in the Moscow hospital, and as he grew gradually weaker, Pierre began keeping his distance. He did not know why, but ever since Karataev had begun to deteriorate, it cost Pierre an effort to go near him. When he did approach and heard the quiet moaning with which Karataev usually lay down at each stopping place, and when he smelled the odor coming from him—now stronger than before—Pierre would move farther away and try not to think about him.

While imprisoned in the shed, Pierre had learned—not through his intellect but with his whole being, through life itself—that human beings are made for happiness, that happiness lies within us in the satisfaction of simple human needs, and that all unhappiness comes not from deprivation but from excess. And now, during these last three weeks of marching, he had learned yet another new and comforting truth: that nothing in this world is truly terrible. He had learned that just as there is no condition in which a person can be completely happy and entirely free, there is no condition in which one must be completely unhappy and lack all freedom. He learned that suffering and freedom have their limits, and that those limits are very close together; that the person lying in a bed of roses with one crumpled petal suffered as keenly as he now did, sleeping on bare damp earth with one side growing cold while the other warmed; and that when he had once worn tight dancing shoes, he had suffered just as much as he did now walking with bare feet covered in sores—his footwear having long since fallen apart. He discovered that when he had married his wife—seemingly of his own free will—he had been no more free than now, when they locked him in a stable at night. Of all the things he later called his sufferings, but which at the time he barely felt, the worst was the state of his bare, raw, scab-covered feet. (The horsemeat was actually appetizing and nourishing; the saltpeter flavor of the gunpowder they used instead of salt was even pleasant; there was no great cold; it was always warm walking during the day; and at night there were campfires; the lice that devoured him actually warmed his body.) The one thing that was initially hard to bear was his feet.

After the second day's march, Pierre examined his feet by the campfire and thought it would be impossible to walk on them. But when everyone got up, he went along limping, and once he had warmed up, walked without feeling the pain, though at night his feet looked more terrible than before. But he no longer looked at them and thought of other things instead.

Only now did Pierre truly grasp the full strength of life in a person and the saving power of being able to shift one's attention from one thing to another—like the safety valve on a boiler that releases excess steam when the pressure becomes too great.

He did not see and did not hear them shooting the prisoners who fell behind, though more than a hundred died that way. He did not think of Karataev, who grew weaker every day and would clearly soon share the same fate. Still less did Pierre think about himself. The harder his situation became and the more terrible the future, the more independent of his circumstances were the joyful and comforting thoughts, memories, and imaginings that came to him.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: You would have thought that under the almost incredibly wretched conditions the Russian soldiers endured—lacking warm boots and sheepskin coats, with no roof over their heads, camping in the snow at eighteen below zero, without even full rations (the supply wagons didn't always keep up with the troops)—they would have presented a sad and depressing sight.

On the contrary, the army had never appeared more cheerful and spirited, not even under the best material conditions. This was because all who began to grow depressed or who lost strength were sifted out of the army day by day. All the physically or mentally weak had long since been left behind; only the best of the army—physically and mentally—remained.

More men gathered behind the wattle fence of the Eighth Company than anywhere else. Two sergeants major sat with them and their campfire blazed brighter than the others. For permission to sit by their wattle, they demanded contributions of firewood.

"Hey, Makeev! Where've you gone, you son of a gun? Are you lost, or have the wolves eaten you? Bring more wood!" shouted a red-haired, red-faced man, squinting and blinking from the smoke but not moving away from the fire. "And you, Jackdaw, go get some wood too!" he said to another soldier.

This red-haired man was neither a sergeant nor a corporal, but being robust, he ordered around those weaker than himself. The soldier they called "Jackdaw," a thin little fellow with a sharp nose, got up obediently and was about to go when the slender, handsome figure of a young soldier carrying a load of wood appeared in the firelight.
"Bring it here—that's the stuff!"

They split up the wood, pressed it down on the fire, blew on it with their mouths, and fanned it with the skirts of their greatcoats, making the flames hiss and crackle. The men drew closer and lit their pipes. The handsome young soldier who had brought the wood set his arms akimbo and began stamping his cold feet rapidly and nimbly on the spot.
"Mother! The dew is cold but clear... It's good that I'm a musketeer..." he sang, pretending to hiccup after each line.
"Watch it, your soles will fly off!" shouted the red-haired man, noticing that the dancer's boot sole was hanging loose. "What a fellow you are for dancing!"
The dancer stopped, pulled off the loose piece of leather, and threw it on the fire.

"Right you are, friend," he said, and having sat down, took a scrap of blue French cloth from his knapsack and wrapped it around his foot. "It's the steam that ruins them," he added, stretching out his feet toward the fire.
"They'll be issuing us new ones soon. They say once we've finished hammering them, we'll get double kits!"
"And that rascal Petrov has fallen behind after all, it seems," said one sergeant major.
"I've had my eye on him for a while," said the other.
"Well, he's a sorry excuse for a soldier..."
"But in the Third Company, they say nine men went missing yesterday."
"Sure, but when a man's feet are frozen, how can he walk?"
"Come on, don't talk nonsense!" said the sergeant major.
"Do you want the same thing to happen to you?" said an old soldier, turning reproachfully to the man who had spoken about frozen feet.

"Well, you know," said the sharp-nosed man they called Jackdaw, in a squeaky, unsteady voice, raising himself on the other side of the fire, "a fat man gets thin, but a thin man—it's death. Take me, for instance! I've got no strength left," he added with sudden determination, turning to the sergeant major. "Tell them to send me to the hospital. I'm aching all over. I won't be able to keep up anyway."
"That'll do, that'll do!" the sergeant major replied quietly.
The soldier said no more and the conversation moved on.
"What a lot of those Frenchies they took today, and the fact is that not one of them had what you'd call real boots," said a soldier, starting a new topic. "They were nothing but fakes."

"The Cossacks took their boots. They were clearing the hut for the colonel and carried them out. It was pitiful to see, boys," the dancer put in. "As they turned them over, one seemed still alive, and would you believe it, he was jabbering something in their language."
"But they're a clean lot, lads," the first man went on. "He was white—white as birchbark—and some of them are such fine-looking fellows, you'd think they were noblemen."
"Well, what do you expect? They make soldiers of all classes over there."
"But they can't understand our language at all," said the dancer with a puzzled smile. "I asked him who his master was, and he just jabbered away in his own way. A strange lot!"

"But here's what's odd, friends," continued the man who had marveled at their whiteness, "the peasants at Mozhaysk were saying that when they started burying the dead—where the battle was, you know—well, the dead had been lying there nearly a month, and the peasant says, 'They lie as white as paper, clean, and not so much smell as a puff of gunpowder.'"
"Was it from the cold?" someone asked.

"Clever fellow! From the cold indeed! It was hot then. If it had been from the cold, ours wouldn't have rotted either. 'But,' he says, 'go up to ours, and they're all rotten and full of maggots. So,' he says, 'we tie cloths over our faces and turn our heads away as we drag them off—we can barely manage it. But theirs,' he says, 'are white as paper and don't smell any more than a whiff of gunpowder.'"
Everyone was silent.
"Must be from their food," said the sergeant major. "They ate the same food as the gentry."
No one disagreed.

"That peasant near Mozhaysk where the battle was said they called up men from ten villages around and carted for twenty days and still didn't finish clearing away the dead. And as for the wolves, he says..."
"That was a real battle," said an old soldier. "It's the only one worth remembering. Everything since then has just been tormenting people."

"And you know what, Daddy—the day before yesterday we charged at them, and my word, they didn't let us get close before they just threw down their muskets and dropped to their knees. 'Pardon!' they say. That's just one example. They say Platov captured Napoleon himself twice. But he didn't know the right magic word. He catches him and catches him—no good! He turns into a bird in his hands and flies away. And there's no way to kill him either."
"You're a first-class liar, Kiselev, I can see that!"
"Liar, nothing! It's the honest truth."
"If he fell into my hands—once I caught him, I'd bury him in the ground with an aspen stake to pin him down. What a lot of people he's destroyed!"
"Well, either way, we're going to finish it. He won't be coming here again," said the old soldier, yawning.
The conversation died down and the soldiers began settling in to sleep.
"Look at the stars. Amazing how they shine! You'd think the women had laid out their linen to dry," said one of the men, gazing admiringly at the Milky Way.
"That's a sign of a good harvest next year."
"We'll need more wood."
"You warm your back and your belly freezes. That's a strange thing."
"Oh Lord!"
"What are you pushing for? Is the fire only for you? Look how he's sprawling!"

In the silence that followed, the snoring of those who had fallen asleep could be heard. Others turned over and warmed themselves, occasionally exchanging a few words. From a campfire a hundred paces away came the sound of loud, merry laughter.
"Listen to them roaring over there in the Fifth Company!" said one of the soldiers. "And what a crowd of them there are!"
One of the men got up and went over to the Fifth Company.
"They're having a great time," he said, coming back. "Two Frenchies have turned up. One's practically frozen, and the other's a real show-off. He's singing songs..."
"Oh, I'll go over and have a look..."
And several of the men went over to the Fifth Company.
